description: The Lone Quasar is a solo team with one backend software engineer. A quasar is a single object that outshines whole galaxies, and that’s the approach here: one person, a focused idea, and a lot of effort. For this challenge, I’m combining my software engineering background with AI-assisted development to turn NASA’s open data into a working, user-friendly app. I’m in it to learn, build something useful, and finish a complete project in one weekend.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink Viewer is a web tool for looking at real SPHEREx infrared images of any patch of sky. You enter a position (RA/Dec) or pick a target, then blink through the images by epoch or by wavelength. You can also combine the images of one epoch, subtract the first epoch to see what changed, and read a spectrum and light curve at that position.

The challenge is to find moving objects like Planet X: something that moves shifts between epochs while the stars stay still.

How it works: a Python pipeline queries NASA’s open IRSA archive for SPHEREx images of the position, subtracts the background, measures the flux, and builds the combined and difference images. A FastAPI service serves them to a small browser app in plain JavaScript. It runs on an AWS EC2 instance.

The five challenge test targets are cached and load instantly. Other positions are built live from the archive, which can be slow or unavailable.

This is a solo project. Anyone can use the tool, no astronomy software needed.
details:
What it does. SPHEREx Blink Viewer shows real SPHEREx infrared images of a patch of sky. Enter RA/Dec or pick a target, then blink through the images by epoch or by wavelength. It can combine the images of one epoch, subtract the first epoch to show what changed, and plot a spectrum and a light curve at the position. Each image shows its date, wavelength and flagged-pixel fraction, and is labelled as real data.

How it works. A Python pipeline (Astropy, reproject, NumPy, Pillow) queries the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive for SPHEREx images of the position, downloads cutouts, subtracts the background, measures the flux, and builds the combined and difference images. A FastAPI service serves them to a browser app written in plain JavaScript (built with Vite). The five challenge test targets (WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) are cached and load instantly; other positions are built live from the archive, which can be slow or unavailable. The site runs on an AWS EC2 instance.

Benefits and impact. A moving object shifts between epochs while the stars stay still, so blinking makes it visible. Anyone can look for moving or changing objects in SPHEREx data with only a browser.

What I considered. Honest labelling (real vs simulated data, an optional background sky image marked as not SPHEREx data), shareable links with the coordinates in the URL, and clear messages when the archive is down.

Team. Solo project. Code and documentation were written with AI assistance (Claude Code); the demo voice-over is AI-generated (ElevenLabs).

Source code. https://github.com/tiendat161/spherex-viewer
